system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Ring Lemma
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: In scope: the statement that radii of circles completely surrounding a circle with M neighbors are comparable with constant depending only on M, the proof idea, and its role in compactness arguments and in bounded-degree geometric estimates. Excluded: applications beyond how it is used to control neighbor radii.

ATOMS:
- MATH-PROB-C07-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Given circles $C_0,C_1,\dots,C_M$ with disjoint interiors, the circles $C_1,\dots,C_M$ completely surround $C_0$ when all of them are tangent to $C_0$ and $C_i$ is tangent to $C_{i+1}$ for $i=1,\dots,M$, where $C_{M+1}$ is set to be $C_1$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0058-s25] Given circles C0, C1, . . . , CM with disjoint interiors, we say that C1, . . . , CM completely surround C0 if they are all tangent to C0 and Ci is tangent to Ci+1 for i = 1, . . . , M (where CM+1 is set to be C1).
- MATH-PROB-C07-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: The Ring Lemma states that for every integer $M>0$ there exists $A>0$ such that, if a circle $C_0$ is completely surrounded by $M$ circles $C_1,\dots,C_M$ and $r_i$ is the radius of $C_i$ for $i=0,1,\dots,M$, then $r_0/r_i \le A$ for every $i=1,\dots,M$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0059-s02] Lemma 4.2 (Ring Lemma, Rodin and Sullivan [70]) For every integer M > 0 there exists A > 0 such that if C0 is a circle completely surrounded by M circles C1, . . . , CM, and ri is the radius of Ci for every i = 0, 1, . . . , M, then r0/ri ≤A for every i = 1, . . . , M.
- MATH-PROB-C07-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: In the proof of the Ring Lemma, after scaling so that $r_0=1$, if a circle $C_2$ among the circles completely surrounding $C_0$ has small radius, then its neighbouring circles $C_1$ and $C_3$ cannot both have large radii compared to $C_2$, because they would intersect, so at least one of them must also be small.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0059-s03] Proof We may scale the picture so that r0 = 1.
    [MATH-PROB-p0059-s04] Assume that the radius of C2 is small and consider the circles C1 and C3 to its left and right.
    [MATH-PROB-p0059-s05] It cannot be that both C1 and C3 have large radii compared to C2 since in this case they will intersect; see Fig. 4.1.
    [MATH-PROB-p0059-s06] Hence, one of them has to be small as well.
    [MATH-PROB-p0059-s08] By similar reasoning, one of C1 and C4 has to be small.
    [MATH-PROB-p0059-s09] We continue this argument this way and get a path of circles of small radii; thus, for the circles C1, . . . , CM to completely surround C0 we learn that M must be large. ⊓⊔
- MATH-PROB-C07-S2-02.r1 | S2
  ATOM: When packings $P_n$ obtained from the circle packing theorem for graphs $G_n$ are scaled and translated so that $\mathrm{rad}(x)=1$ and $\mathrm{cent}(x)$ is the origin, the Ring Lemma gives a constant $A=A(x,y)>0$ with $A^{-1}\le \mathrm{rad}(y)\le A$ for the vertex $y$ under consideration, and by compactness there is a subsequence $P_{n_k}$ along which both $\mathrm{rad}_{n_k}(y)$ and $\mathrm{cent}_{n_k}(y)$ converge.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0059-s18] Apply the circle packing theorem to Gn to obtain a packing Pn, and scale and translate it so that rad(x) = 1 and cent(x) is the origin.
    [MATH-PROB-p0059-s20] By the Ring Lemma (Lemma 4.2), there exists a constant A = A(x, y) > 0 such that A−1 ≤rad(y) ≤A.
    [MATH-PROB-p0059-s21] By compactness there exists a subsequence of packings Pnk for which radnk(y) and centnk(y) both converge.
- MATH-PROB-C07-S2-03.r1 | S2
  ATOM: In a circle packing where the circle $C_{v_0}$ is centered at the origin, every vertex $v\in V_R$ satisfies $\mathrm{rad}(v)\le R$. For such $v$, the Ring Lemma gives a constant $A=A(\Delta)$ such that $\mathrm{rad}(u)\le AR$ for every neighbor $u\sim v$, and therefore $|\mathrm{cent}(u)|\le (A+2)R$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0062-s12] For every v ∈VR it holds that rad(v) ≤R since Cv0 is centered at the origin.
    [MATH-PROB-p0062-s13] By the Ring Lemma (Lemma 4.2), there exists A = A(Δ) such that rad(u) ≤AR for every u ∼v , and therefore | cent(u)| ≤(A + 2)R.
- MATH-PROB-C07-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Double circle packings, which apply to polyhedral planar graphs (simple and 3-connected planar graphs), also satisfy a version of the ring lemma.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0112-s05] If one wishes to study planar graphs that are not triangulations, it is often convenient to work with double circle packings, which enjoy similar rigidity properties to usual circle packings, but for the larger class of polyhedral planar graphs.
    [MATH-PROB-p0112-s06] Here, a planar graph is polyhedral if it is both simple and 3-connected, meaning that the removal of any two vertices cannot disconnect the graph.
    [MATH-PROB-p0112-s07] Double circle packings also satisfy a version of the ring lemma [45, Theorem 4.1], which means that they can be used to produce good straightline embeddings of polyhedral planar graphs that have bounded face degrees but which are not necessarily triangulations.
- MATH-PROB-C07-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Unlike circle packings, square tilings of planar graphs do not enjoy an analogue of the Ring Lemma.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0114-s06] Unlike circle packing, however, square tilings do not enjoy an analogue of the ring lemma, and can be geometrically very degenerate.
- MATH-PROB-C07-S3-03.r1a | S3
  ATOM: Square tilings, unlike circle packings, do not enjoy an analogue of the Ring Lemma.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0114-s06] Unlike circle packing, however, square tilings do not enjoy an analogue of the ring lemma, and can be geometrically very degenerate.
- MATH-PROB-C07-S3-03.r1b | S3
  ATOM: Square tilings can be geometrically very degenerate.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0114-s06] Unlike circle packing, however, square tilings do not enjoy an analogue of the ring lemma, and can be geometrically very degenerate.
